Third, a data reduction framework is introduced to mitigate issues of excessive data volume and redundant features by reducing both features and attribute values, thus improving recognition accuracy and reducing storage requirements. Finally, case studies on wind power installations under extreme cold and typhoon threats in two regions of China are conducted. Results show that the average deviation between resilience evaluations based on reduced data and full data is within 5%, while data storage is reduced by 35.8%. This provides data-driven decision support for wind farm managers and alleviates challenges posed by large data volumes.

title: An Overlap-Aware Rectification Deep Neural Network with Dual-Branch Architecture for Gearbox Open-Set Fault Diagnosis
exported_title: An overlap-aware rectification deep neural network with dual-branch architecture for gearbox open-set fault diagnosis

metadata.abstract: Open-set fault diagnosis (OSFD) requires accurate recognition of known faults while rejecting unseen fault categories, but feature overlap near decision boundaries can cause both false rejection and false acceptance. This study proposes an Overlap-Aware Rectification Network (OAR-Net) that combines multi-scale feature extraction, dual-branch metric learning, and a three-stage decision strategy. Samples with clear Mahalanobis-distance evidence are directly accepted or rejected, whereas samples in the intermediate buffer region are further evaluated using prediction uncertainty, local manifold inconsistency, inter-class distance ambiguity, and boundary position. Experiments on the Southeast University (SEU) and Chongqing University (CQU) gearbox datasets show that OAR-Net achieves average OA, UDR, and F1 values of 98.93%, 99.32%, and 99.13%, respectively, on SEU, and 99.01%, 99.31%, and 98.99%, respectively, on CQU. On SEU, OAR-Net improves average OA and F1 by 2.52 and 2.61 percentage points, respectively, over FDML, the strongest baseline by average OA. Cross-speed experiments further show that OAR-Net maintains relatively stable performance under smaller speed variations, although performance degrades as the speed discrepancy increases. These results support the effectiveness of overlap-aware staged verification for gearbox OSFD.

title: OceanPathRL: Deep reinforcement learning-based energy-efficient route optimization system for autonomous electric vessels
exported_title: OceanPathRL: Deep reinforcement learning-based energy-efficient route optimization system for autonomous electric vessels

metadata.abstract: Autonomous electric vessels operating in complex maritime environments must simultaneously optimize energy consumption, maintain regulatory compliance, and coordinate with multiple vessels in real time, yet no existing framework addresses all three objectives within a unified learning architecture. This paper presents OceanPathRL, a novel deep reinforcement learning framework for energy-efficient route optimization in autonomous electric vessels. We propose a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture that integrates Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) with attention-based neural networks and a COLREGs-compliant reward formulation to enable real-time path planning under dynamic ocean conditions, including wave energy prediction and photovoltaic uncertainty management. Extensive evaluations on two publicly available benchmarks, namely the Singapore Maritime Dataset and the MarineCadastre AIS dataset, demonstrate that OceanPathRL achieves a 34.7% reduction in energy consumption compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining a 99.2% collision avoidance success rate and 98.0% COLREGs compliance across head-on, crossing, overtaking, and multi-vessel encounter scenarios. The proposed meta-learning transfer mechanism reduces adaptation steps to new maritime environments by approximately 72.8% relative to conventional training, corresponding to a 3.68× average speedup. These results establish OceanPathRL as a practical and scalable solution for next-generation autonomous maritime systems, directly contributing to the International Maritime Organization decarbonization targets and advancing the field toward deployable, regulation-aware autonomous navigation.

title: A diffusion model-enhanced deep state-space model for RUL prediction
exported_title: A diffusion model-enhanced deep state-space model for RUL prediction

metadata.abstract: Multisensor degradation data typically exhibit high dimensionality, strong noise, and nonlinear evolution, which pose challenges to existing Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction methods in terms of degradation representation learning, temporal modeling, and predictive uncertainty quantification. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Diffusion-Enhanced Deep State-Space Model (Diff-SSM) trained under a two-stage strategy. In the first stage, a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) integrated with a convolutional block attention module (CBAM) is pretrained in a self-supervised manner to extract deep degradation representations that are robust to noise and sensitive to degradation evolution. In the second stage, the learned degradation representations drive a deep state-space model. Specifically, a gated recurrent unit (GRU) constructs the state equation to model temporal degradation evolution, while a variational autoencoder (VAE) constructs the observation equation by mapping the latent variable to the conditional distribution of RUL. Within a variational inference framework, the diffusion feature extractor and the deep state-space model are jointly optimized end-to-end, enabling unified learning of degradation representation extraction, temporal modeling, and RUL inference. Finally, Monte Carlo sampling yields RUL point estimates and prediction intervals. Experiments on the C-MAPSS and PHM2010 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Evaluating the uncertainty anisotropy in flight trajectory prediction using Bayesian Neural Network and SHapley Additive exPlanations
exported_title: Evaluating the uncertainty anisotropy in flight trajectory prediction using Bayesian Neural Network and SHapley Additive exPlanations

metadata.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for flight trajectory prediction in safety-critical Air Traffic Control (ATC) systems. Existing uncertainty quantification methods for flight trajectory prediction often focus on overall uncertainty magnitude or prediction interval coverage, while the spatial anisotropy of predictive uncertainty remains insufficiently investigated. This study first provides empirical evidence that flight trajectory prediction uncertainty is inherently anisotropic, with substantially different uncertainty distributions across longitude, latitude, and altitude. Based on this observation, uncertainty anisotropy is introduced as a complementary evaluation dimension for assessing the quality of uncertainty quantification. A Bayesian Seq-Seq-LSTM framework is developed to jointly predict flight trajectories and quantify predictive uncertainty, and three anisotropy metrics are proposed to quantitatively evaluate the uncertainty anisotropy. Furthermore, SHAP is used to quantify the contributions of input features to model predictions, and the resulting feature-importance patterns are examined alongside the observed uncertainty anisotropy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves better prediction accuracy and uncertainty estimation. Compared with baseline models exhibiting either weak or extreme anisotropy, the proposed framework produces a more moderate degree of uncertainty anisotropy. These findings further demonstrate that uncertainty anisotropy can serve as a complementary evaluation criterion for assessing the physical consistency and reliability of uncertainty estimation in flight trajectory prediction models.

title: SMARF: a semantic memory compression and data-driven prototype-consistency reasoning framework for fault diagnosis based on edge-side small models
exported_title: SMARF: a semantic memory compression and data-driven prototype-consistency reasoning framework for fault diagnosis based on edge-side small models

metadata.abstract: Reliable industrial fault diagnosis with small language models requires traceable evidence, effective retention of temporal context, and stable diagnostic decisions. This study proposes SMARF, a framework that coordinates semantic memory compression and prototype-consistency ranking under a limited context budget. Schema-constrained Semantic Logs link multimodal observations, operating states, and standardized residuals to their evidence sources. A diagnosis-specific memory hierarchy retains temporal evidence through condition-, trend-, and candidate-aware organization. Candidate diagnoses are ranked by combining semantic confidence, retrieved-memory relevance, and training-derived prototype consistency, while uncertainty-guided feedback directs subsequent evidence processing. Using Qwen3-1.7B, SMARF was evaluated on aviation-pump recordings and the UCI Hydraulic Systems dataset. Under 11-fold leave-one-file-out evaluation, SMARF correctly classified all 11 held-out files containing internal operating-state variation, matching the best comparison methods in file-level accuracy and achieving the lowest observed file-level log loss of 0.0538. Correct file decisions were maintained across ten tested seeds and five local sensitivity configurations. Under the strict grouped UCI protocol, SMARF achieved a task-average Macro-F1 of 0.861 across four component-state recognition tasks, with a 95% group-bootstrap confidence interval of [0.839, 0.881]. These results support the value of coordinated semantic memory and statistical consistency checks for fault diagnosis, combining accurate predictions with traceable intermediate evidence and stable decisions under the evaluated conditions.

title: Human-centred risk assessment for port operations using a data-driven approach
exported_title: Human-centred risk assessment for port operations using a data-driven approach

metadata.abstract: Port operations are undergoing rapid digitalisation and automation, yet existing port safety studies remain limited in explaining how human, organisational, and machinery-related factors contribute to different casualty types. This study identifies key contributing risk factors in reported port accidents and develops an exploratory quantitative framework for casualty-type analysis. Using 77 historical accident reports as the development dataset, an accident-report-driven framework integrating LASSO regression with a Tree-Augmented Naive Bayes (TAN) network was constructed. Separate bootstrap stability assessments, repeated nested cross-validation, and supplementary external assessment were conducted. The study makes three contributions: (1) it identifies risk-factor patterns associated with different casualty types; (2) it applies a LASSO–TAN framework to model conditional dependencies among selected factors; (3) it conducts scenario analysis to support casualty-specific accident interpretation and hypothesis generation. The results indicate that equipment type, safeguards, cargo type, safety warnings, and ergonomic conditions are the principal predictors retained within the analysed dataset. Machinery-related injury and fall-from-height MPE configurations share container cargo, unclear warnings, poor ergonomic conditions, and non-adopted safeguards, but differ in equipment type. The findings support retrospective accident interpretation rather than accident-occurrence prediction or claims of intervention effectiveness.

title: A risk-aware surrogate Bayesian optimization framework driven by spatial generalized extreme value model for urban road network simulation calibration
exported_title: A risk-aware surrogate Bayesian optimization framework driven by spatial generalized extreme value model for urban road network simulation calibration

metadata.abstract: Traffic simulation serves as a prerequisite support for the engineering application of research in the safety domain in urban road networks. To reproduce the spatial crash risk field, calibrating traffic simulations at the urban road network level is a complex and systematic task. Challenges remain in replicating traffic safety via such simulations, especially when safety is dominated by extreme vehicle interactions rather than average traffic conflicts. Generally, the spatial heterogeneity of crash risk in urban road networks is mainly associated with origin-destination demand, extreme traffic conflicts, and driver behavior. However, existing methods often consider these factors independently, which limits their ability to capture spatial crash risk patterns. Given this, this study proposes a risk-aware surrogate Bayesian optimization framework driven by spatial generalized extreme value model for urban road network simulation calibration. This framework considers origin-destination demand representation, spatial extreme crash risk modeling, and heterogeneous driver behavior calibration. The results show that: (i) the framework ensures consistency between simulated and observed traffic volumes; (ii) it improves the fidelity of extreme events by reproducing the lower tail of traffic conflict distributions. From a systematic perspective, this study serves as a pioneering study for the coordinated control oriented toward safety and resilience.
